content: The 2010 World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines on infant feeding in the context of HIV recommended exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) for the first six months of life, followed by complementary feeding and continued breastfeeding up to one year of age. This recommendation was made under the condition that either the mother or the infant was receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) to prevent mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV. However, at the time these guidelines were developed, there was limited data on the risk of postnatal HIV transmission in women who were on ART during pregnancy and continued treatment after delivery, or in infants who received ART prophylaxis. Over the past five years, additional evidence has emerged from studies and programs that achieved PMTCT through maternal ART or infant antiretroviral (ARV) prophylaxis. Despite this, the precise risk of HIV transmission and infant mortality (HIV-free survival) in such programs remains unclear. It is also uncertain whether mixed feeding (combining breastfeeding with other foods or liquids) continues to pose a higher risk of HIV transmission compared to exclusive breastfeeding, as was observed in the pre-ART era, or whether effective ARV treatment reduces transmission risk to negligible levels regardless of feeding practices. In October 2015, WHO convened a guideline review meeting to reassess the 2010 recommendations on HIV and infant feeding in light of the increasing use of ART among pregnant and breastfeeding women. One of the key questions addressed was the relationship between infant feeding practices, particularly the duration of breastfeeding, and HIV-free survival in infants born to mothers on ART. To inform this discussion, a systematic review and GRADE evidence summary tables were prepared. The systematic review focused on HIV-free survival at 12, 18, and 24 months in infants born to women on ART, stratified by infant feeding modality. Data on overall HIV transmission, transmission by six months of age, and HIV-free survival by feeding modality were also analyzed. A second review, presented separately, summarized evidence on breastfeeding practices during the first six months of life, with HIV transmission at six and 12 months as outcomes. Methods The review included both experimental and observational studies, such as randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, and longitudinal studies. Eligible participants were HIV-positive mothers receiving ART and their breastfed infants, with some infants also receiving prophylactic ARVs as per the 2010 WHO guidelines. The primary outcomes were HIV-free survival and HIV transmission between birth and 24 months of age. A comprehensive search of English-language literature from 2005 to 2015 was conducted using databases such as PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, and CINAHL. Conference abstracts and grey literature were also reviewed. Authors of relevant studies were contacted for additional information when necessary. Results Eighteen cohort studies were included in the analysis, seven of which were nested within randomized clinical trials. Most studies followed mothers receiving ART for PMTCT, with recommendations for exclusive breastfeeding for six months followed by rapid weaning, in line with WHO guidelines at the time. In some studies, ART was discontinued after breastfeeding cessation, while others provided lifelong ART regardless of CD4 count and supported breastfeeding for 12 months. The quality of the included studies was assessed using a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). HIV-free survival was assessed at various time points, with some studies excluding early deaths or HIV transmissions within the first days or weeks of life. Key Findings 1. HIV-Free Survival by Feeding Modality: Studies comparing HIV-free survival between breastfed and formula-fed infants showed mixed results. Some studies reported higher HIV-free survival rates among breastfed infants, while others found no significant difference. Mixed feeding (breastfeeding combined with other foods or liquids) was associated with higher HIV transmission risk in some studies, but this risk appeared to be mitigated by effective maternal ART. 2. Duration of ART and Breastfeeding: HIV-free survival rates were generally higher in infants whose mothers were on lifelong ART compared to those whose mothers received ART only up to six months postpartum. The timing of ART initiation during pregnancy varied across studies, with some starting as early as 14–15 weeks of gestation and others initiating ART between 24 and 36 weeks. 3. HIV Transmission and Mortality: HIV transmission rates were lower in studies where mothers received lifelong ART. However, some studies reported post-weaning HIV transmission, particularly when ART was discontinued after breastfeeding cessation. Infant mortality patterns varied, with some studies reporting higher deaths after weaning, while others observed no significant difference before and after weaning. 4. HIV-Free Survival at 12, 18, and 24 Months: HIV-free survival rates at 12 months ranged from 82% to 96%, depending on the study and ART duration. At 18 months, HIV-free survival rates were slightly lower but not significantly different from 12-month estimates. At 24 months, HIV-free survival rates ranged from 83% to 97%, with variations based on maternal ART duration and feeding practices. Limitations The quality of evidence was rated as low to very low due to the observational nature of most studies, inconsistencies in reporting feeding practices, and lack of direct alignment with the PICO question. Some studies did not provide detailed information on feeding modalities, and others excluded early endpoints, making comparisons challenging. Conclusion The systematic review highlights the importance of maternal ART in achieving high rates of HIV-free survival among breastfed infants. Lifelong ART appears to provide better outcomes compared to ART limited to the breastfeeding period. However, further research is needed to clarify the impact of mixed feeding and to optimize feeding recommendations in the context of maternal ART.
